title: What Is the Marketplace Economy? A Payout Guide

## What Is the Marketplace Economy?


The marketplace economy operates as a decentralized business model. Digital services act as matchmakers connecting buyers directly with independent sellers and service providers.


This structure differs from standard retail, and it's the model behind modern[marketplace services](https://usedots.com/solutions/marketplaces/) that own zero inventory and hire no direct workforce. Instead, they provide the digital infrastructure where supply meets demand. The division of labor is clear:


- The digital service handles the search, booking, and initial transaction.
- The independent provider delivers the actual service or product to the buyer.
- The payout infrastructure routes the earnings directly to the provider.


## The Shift Toward a Global Gig Workforce


Independent talent drives the[gig economy marketplace](https://usedots.com/solutions/gig-economy/) . This pool continues expanding past local borders and evolving into a global workforce. The World Bank estimates that there are between[154 million and 435 million](https://gfmag.com/banking/cross-border-payments-adapt-to-gig-economy/) gig workers worldwide. This massive base of freelancers forces digital services to rethink how they process payouts. Treat contractor payouts as core product infrastructure and build on a global payments API from day one, because retrofitting country-by-country payout logic after launch costs far more than designing for it up front.


When your service relies on manual spreadsheets or legacy bank portals, paying a global workforce quickly becomes impossible. You need integrated infrastructure that routes funds automatically across hundreds of jurisdictions. This setup lets you verify identities and collect tax documentation before any money moves.


## How to Send Money to Gig Workers Across Borders


Moving high-volume, low-value payouts across borders breaks legacy banking. You face unpredictable settlement delays, complex currency conversions, and disconnected[local payment rails](https://usedots.com/blog/ach-rtp-swift-payment-rails/) .


Standard international wires destroy the unit economics of global gig work. Sending money internationally costs[6.5% on average](https://interledger.org/blog/cross-border-micropayments-interledger/) . For smaller payouts, this percentage markup quickly consumes a large portion of a gig worker's earnings. You can bypass these expensive channels and protect small balances from fee erosion by using a[payouts API](https://usedots.com/platform/payouts-api/) with automated jurisdiction-aware routing to move funds through more than 300 local payment networks, including real time payments rails such as RTP (the US Real-Time Payments network) and FedNow (the Federal Reserve's instant payment service).

## How to Automate Contractor Payouts at Scale


In the gig economy marketplace, manual spreadsheet workflows collapse under high-volume transactions. Bulk uploads to standard bank portals introduce human error, which slows settlement times and creates massive reconciliation headaches when processing a high volume of[payouts](https://usedots.com/blog/what-is-a-payout/) for your finance team.


Scaling contractor payouts demands an API-driven infrastructure with[automated payouts](https://usedots.com/platform/payouts-automation/) at its core. You need integrated systems that release funds instantly upon verified milestones. When a seller finalizes a transaction, the underlying codebase triggers an API call that routes funds directly to the payee in seconds, and each response returns a status you can match to your ledger for real time reconciliation. This programmatic approach bypasses manual bank portals entirely, removing the administrative burden from your finance team while giving your workforce instant access to their earnings.


The math shows why. A service sending 10,000 payouts a month with a 2% manual error rate has 200 payments to trace and resend every month.


## Managing Payee Onboarding and Identity Verification


You cannot pay a distributed workforce in the marketplace economy without verifying who sits on the receiving end. Operating a compliant digital service demands mandatory identity checks before a single dollar moves. You must execute[KYC (Know Your Customer) verification](https://usedots.com/blog/what-is-kyc-banking-payouts/) protocols for individual gig workers and KYB (Know Your Business) validation for entity sellers.


Your[onboarding flow](https://usedots.com/platform/onboard/) must stop bad actors while keeping legitimate earners moving. Lengthy manual reviews cause contractor churn and introduce multi-week onboarding delays before a single payout clears. You need an automated system that executes liveness detection and blocks AI-generated face spoofing instantly. This setup verifies legitimate payees in seconds so they can access their earnings without friction.


## Automating Tax Compliance for Sellers and Providers


The administrative burden of paying non-employees scales aggressively as your gig economy marketplace grows. Every independent seller, from marketplace vendors to[freelancer payouts](https://usedots.com/solutions/freelancers/) , introduces strict tax reporting obligations, which your finance team must execute before any funds clear. Treat tax collection as an afterthought, and you invite severe penalties.


Tax documentation must live inside your payment flow to remove the manual chase entirely. This infrastructure requires specific components:


- **US contractors:** Execute upfront TIN (Taxpayer Identification Number) matching before any payout batch clears. Catching mismatches early acts as a structural defense against IRS CP2100 notices, which trigger mandatory[24% backup withholding](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/backup-withholding) on future payments to a flagged worker. You must collect a W-9 (US tax identification form) before the first payment clears, because once cumulative payments to a U.S. contractor cross $2,000 in a calendar year, IRC §6041 requires a 1099-NEC (nonemployee compensation) filing. That threshold applies to payments made after December 31, 2025, and was $600 before then,[according to the IRS](https://www.irs.gov/faqs/small-business-self-employed-other-business/form-1099-nec-independent-contractors/form-1099-nec-independent-contractors) . Miss it and you face penalties up to[$310 per unfiled form](https://www.irs.gov/payments/information-return-penalties) under IRC §6722.
- **International contractors:** Automatically collect W-8BENs (foreign status certification forms) during onboarding to certify non-US status and bypass mandatory withholding.
